speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In today’s world, where divisions and distrust are rising, preserving trust and safeguarding racial and religious harmony are more important than ever.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many societies, including ours, are facing challenges such as misinformation, external influences and global conflicts that can strain social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In such times, it is not just the responsibility of the Government but also of community organisations and the general public to work together to defend our unity.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Government plays a critical role in setting the legal and policy framework, but policies alone are not enough.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: True harmony comes from the everyday actions of our people.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Community organisations can lead the way by creating safe spaces for dialogue, encouraging interfaith understanding and addressing concerns before they escalate into divisions.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The public, too, has a powerful role to play.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Simple acts, like respecting different religious practices, learning about other cultures, and standing up against discrimination, help build a more inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In an era where divisive rhetoric spreads easily online, responsible sharing of information is key to ensuring that harmony is not undermined by falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, for any society to stay united, trust in public institutions, especially those responsible for law and order, is essential.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Yet, across the world, many institutions are suffering from a trust deficit.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Concerns about transparency, fairness, and accountability have led to a declining confidence in governments and law enforcement agencies.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is a worrying trend because when people lose trust in institutions, they turn to alternative sources, sometimes unreliable or even harmful ones.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore has largely maintained high levels of trust in its institutions, but we must not take this for granted.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One lesson we can learn from other countries is the importance of proactive engagement.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Defending racial and religious harmony is a shared responsibility.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While the Government provides policies and enforcement, community organisations and individuals must actively contribute to a culture of mutual respect and understanding.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At the same time, strengthening trust in institutions, especially those responsible for law and order, is vital for a stable and united society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Public institutions globally are suffering from a trust deficit.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In today’s digital world, technology is a double-edged sword.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It drives progress but also enables new forms of crime, from cyberattacks to online scams and misinformation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To stay ahead, we must harness technology and strengthen partnerships across sectors.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Governments must invest in artificial intelligence (AI)-driven threat detection, advanced cybersecurity frameworks and digital forensics.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Collaboration between law enforcement, tech companies and the public is crucial.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Public education on digital risks, real-time information sharing, and international cooperation can enhance our ability to tackle these evolving threats.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: By combining innovation with strong partnerships, we can build a safer, more resilient society in the face of emerging security challenges.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How is the Home Team helping its officers to develop new skills and capabilities so that they can utilise the new technology and remain ready to address emerging security challenges?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With the rise in cybercrime, how is the Home Team enhancing its partnerships with the community and members of the public to promote safety and security in both the digital and physical space?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Singapore actively participates in such fora and regularly shares our experience with counterparts internationally and I support such moves across borders to take a firm stance against such malicious and downright criminal actions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My cut will focus on how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), through improving deepfake technology, is able to supercharge the effects of online violence against individual.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I am mindful that some in this House have been victims of such deepfake online violence and have reported these matters to the relevant authorities, and wish to acknowledge the real harm that such actions have on all victims.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My cut today will focus on areas where I feel special attention is warranted.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There is increasing acknowledgement that because of their young age and still developing brain, children are more vulnerable to the long-lasting psychological damage caused by harmful deepfakes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Victims of such crimes end up with significant distress, anxiety and depression, and some even experience post-traumatic stress disorder.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There is also often a long tail of effects that stretch beyond social and emotional damage, especially as these child victims sometimes end up being unable to attend school because they are suffering so much.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While both males and females have been victims, women are still very much the overwhelming target of deepfakes, particularly those involving sexually explicit images.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Some commentators are also worried about the weaponisation of AI against women, particularly when facial search engines can scoop up these deepfake images and link them to one's Internet identity for a long time.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There is thus concern about a chill effect on women's career progression.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Even more alarmingly, nine in 10 women restrict their online activity in an attempt to protect themselves.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This increases the digital gender divide and limits access to employment, education, healthcare and community through digital spaces directly correlating with lost career opportunities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This also has implications on our efforts to get more women into politics.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A 2024 Oxford study notes that women may be discouraged from running for public office when female politicians are targeted.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A fellow delegate at a Commonwealth Parliamentary Association conference on AI and misinformation last year shared that when both female and male politicians in his country fell victim to sexually explicit deepfakes, hardly anyone clicked on the links for the male politician while the deepfake content for the female politician went viral.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There is thus, clearly, a gender perspective to harms caused by AI that we need to be mindful of and our measures to deal with the problems has to address these.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There was also an announcement of a new agency to tackle online harms announced by Prime Minister Wong in October last year, as a joint Ministry of Digital Development and Information (MDDI) and Ministry of Law effort.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I support this as no victim should have to submit individual take down requests.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Equally welcome are the laws that MDDI announced will be introduced to allow victims to file civil claims against their perpetrators and I look forward to hearing more details about these upcoming changes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I asked the Minister for Home Affairs in August 2024 to consider an anti-scam centre-like model, to allow a centralised response to deepfake related crimes and hope that the new online harms agency can be the base from which we work and include both psychological support and education.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our officers handling such cases should be given regular and updated training to support victims of such crimes from a victim-centric approach, as some may feel hesitant reporting such crimes out of shame or fear of inadvertently triggering the Streisand effect.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It should also be easy for victims to be channelled to train mental health professionals to support them throughout the entire process.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For education, it is crucial that agencies also work across departments to ensure that both children and adults are aware of the real harms that such deepfakes can cause.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: According to the Singapore Police Forces Annual Road Traffic Situation 2023 and 2024 reports, the number of traffic accidents is on an upward trend.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Who are the most vulnerable on our roads?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I propose greater public participation with incentives to nudge road users to drive safely.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would the Ministry consider encouraging road users to report to the Traffic Police, with video evidence, unsafe, negligent or rash road behaviour committed against motorcyclists and elderly pedestrians?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If summonses are issued to and paid by errant road users, a percentage of the summons amount, after accounting for administrative costs, can be given to the person who first reported the incident to incentivise the reporting of unsafe road practises.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such an approach will significantly supplement Traffic Police enforcement operations, particularly in view of the national manpower challenge.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A similar approach can be taken towards drivers who transport foreign workers in lorries.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Should they speed or drive in an unsafe manner, road users should be encouraged to report such behaviour and should expect to receive some percentage of the fine amount for their act of civic consciousness.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is for the act of reporting on these episodes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, can the Minister tell us whether the Traffic Police would consider reintroducing the blinking amber light that used to be commonly seen on the top of cabins of commercial vehicles, so that road users can be alerted to commercial vehicles carrying goods and foreign workers more easily?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some of them could not recall receiving letters from the Traffic Police about the matter.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Others recounted receiving the letters, but explained that they had problems using Singpass to attach their medical reports or had tried unsuccessfully to seek clarification through emails to the Traffic Police (TP).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From my observations, a driver whose licence has expired may not be aware of this.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The problem becomes incurable when the licence has lapsed for three years or more.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This came as a shock to some residents.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I feel that this area deserves review in two aspects.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, could the age at which medical reports are required be moved to a later age?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: With better nutrition and health, and Singaporeans working longer, we could look at requiring medical examinations later.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Second, it would be better if TP could issue a final letter to seniors once their driving licences have expired for two years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The letter should remind them that if they do not renew their licence within the next one year, they will not be able to do so.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, in today's volatile global landscape and with recent reports of far-right extremism, even in our midst, we must acknowledge that this precious harmony cannot be taken for granted.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We do not inherit harmony, we continue to build on it.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is therefore incumbent on all of us to remain vigilant in preserving this unity.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I would therefore like to ask the Ministry for its assessment of the current state of racial and religious relations, and how our agencies are anticipating emerging threats in this space.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have seen how technology and social media can amplify divisive ideologies, enabling dangerous actors to find like-minded communities or target the vulnerable with disinformation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this fight against extremism, it is essential that stakeholders – community groups, religious organisations, educational institutions and the general public – partner with the Government.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Community organisations can serve as first responders on the ground, spotting early warning signs and offering constructive channels for dialogue.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Religious leaders can build bridges of understanding through inter-faith activities, fostering trust and empathy among different communities.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The public, too, has a critical role to play: by promoting open conversations, reporting suspicious activities and rejecting hateful rhetoric, whenever it arises.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As we continue to navigate an increasingly complex security environment, may we always be guided by vigilance, empathy and unity.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I therefore seek the Ministry's views on how we may deepen our collective efforts to safeguard Singapore's social harmony, ensuring that future generations can inherit a society bound together by respect and mutual understanding.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, while Singapore generally remains a safe and harmonious place, maintaining racial and religious harmony requires ongoing work.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These Bills give the Government a new set of tools to deal with racial and religious harmony.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In previous years, we had seen people arrested who were self-radicalised by materials from violent religious groups online.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What is the Ministry's assessment of the main threats to racial and religious relations in Singapore and what actions does it plan to take in response?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, as Singapore's emergency services demand grows with an ageing population and rising health concerns, the Singapore Civil Defence Forces (SCDF) may face challenges in maintaining a robust and ready workforce.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Emergency personnel are entrusted with the urgent and crucial task of providing life-saving medical treatment during emergencies.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is imperative that they go through a stringent selection process, which includes an assessment of medical training and relevant certifications and familiarity with healthcare protocols, emergency procedures and cultural expectations.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How will SCDF assure the public that this approach will complement rather than displace our local workforce?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: By focusing on workforce development, the transformation will ensure that Home Team agencies are equipped with the skills and expertise needed to address evolving security threats.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This initiative will not only strengthen operational capabilities but will also foster innovation and enable the Home Team to effectively safeguard the nation, while also adapting to technological advancements and dynamic changes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: On that note, how is the Ministry fostering education and lifelong learning among Home Team members to ensure that they are prepared for future challenges, while also supporting their personal and professional development?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Rehabilitation and reintegration into the community are crucial steps in the recovery journey for former drug users, particularly those transiting from custody.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is important that we have in place initiatives designed to support this process, including initiatives that target the unique needs of female drug users.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: On that note, how is the Ministry addressing the specific needs of female drug users; and how can we strengthen community partnerships to effectively lower recidivism rates; and what part can social services, and the wider community, play in bolstering support for innovative initiatives within the halfway house system?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Yellow Ribbon Singapore has made good strides in supporting ex-offenders to upskill and develop careers through initiatives, such as giving ex-offenders who secured jobs through YRSG up to 12 months of career coaching and support.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Nonetheless, some ex-offenders could find it challenging to cope and thus leave these jobs.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: What more can MHA do to prepare and support inmates in their desistance journey?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In my interactions in the Labour Movement with ex-offenders and inmates, they hope when they leave prison to be given an opportunity to rebuild their lives with dignity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We need to invest in the three Rs of rehabilitation: raising their employability and employment opportunities, and re-integrating them back into their families and the community.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is about creating a community where everyone, regardless of their past, has a chance to contribute and thrive.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I applaud the work of Yellow Ribbon Singapore and the many voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs) and groups that have stepped forward and up to help this vulnerable segment of our community.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Can MHA provide an update on what we have done and how far have we come thus far and whether laws such as the Registration of Criminals Act can be reviewed to offer them second chances and have their records spent earlier?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Vikram Nair, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Chairman, in many parts of the world, drug use is a problem getting out of control.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Even in developed countries like the US, the opioid crisis haunts many of its largest cities.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Thousands of lives are ruined by the ready availability of drugs all over the world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Singapore has remained a relative oasis against this scourge thanks to a combination of strong laws, including the death penalty, against drug trafficking.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Strong enforcement of the laws and national education as well support these measures.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Singapore's rates of drug addiction have been amongst the lowest in the world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Do these figures suggest growing drug use amongst youths?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: What are MHA's strategies for dealing with the rise of drug use amongst youths in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Chairman, Singapore is amongst the safest cities in the world and we are proud of our low crime rates.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Unfortunately, one area of vulnerability for us has been scams.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: In recent years, MHA has taken a variety of measures to combat scams, including better education and publicity, rolling out the ScamShield app and engaging in cooperation internationally to try and crack down on scam operators.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Notwithstanding these measures, it appears the problem continues to grow and scammers are thriving.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The most recent measures include action being taken against Singaporeans who may have assisted foreign scammers, including those who help with opening bank accounts that are being used to facilitate scams.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Would the MHA consider taking stricter measures to better detect and deter local Singaporeans from assisting scam operations, in particular, by being money mules?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: In some ways, this is similar to the measures we have taken against drug traffickers and illegal moneylenders.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: While we may be unable to take action against foreign principals, by taking a zero-tolerance approach against their agents in Singapore, we managed to bring both of those problems under better control.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I understand from previous COS debates that the transnational nature of scams makes it difficult to both combat scams and recover the victims' assets.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Does the MHA have any further thoughts on how this may be addressed?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: More young people are experimenting with drugs, often influenced by social media and peer pressure.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: We must strengthen early intervention, working closely with schools, parents and community partners, and rehabilitation must also be a priority.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Prevention, enforcement and rehabilitation must go hand in hand.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Can the Minister share what steps are being taken to ensure our youths stay drug free and have a future full of promise?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Messaging apps and social media platforms remain a keyway for scammers to reach victims.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Many Members of Parliament (MPs) have had fake social media accounts created in our names.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I want to share a recent personal experience.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Recently, others have reported a fake Facebook page in my name.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Residents have told me they have received friend-requests and messages from my Facebook page, asking for their email addresses and other personal details, which I find alarming.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: My experience is probably a drop in the ocean.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Could MHA update on how cooperative messaging apps and social media platforms have been in combating scams?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim
text: Effectively, countering these threats requires collaboration among government bodies, tech companies and international partners.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim
text: On that note, what strategies are currently being employed by the Ministry to identify and respond to the new and emerging threats in a timely and effective manner?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim
text: How is the Ministry working with tech companies and international partners to address the multifaceted nature of scams, and how can the community contribute to the fighting against scams?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, scams continue to be a pressing concern in our digital age.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: As technology evolves, so do the tactics of scammers, who increasingly exploit messaging apps and social media to deceive victims.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Despite ongoing public awareness efforts and enhanced security measures, scams continue to remain persistent and a costly issue.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Given the ease with which scammers infiltrate these platforms, it is crucial that we ensure a strong and coordinated response.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: How are social media and messaging platforms being held accountable for scam activities on their networks?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Chairman, I rise again this year to raise the pressing and worrying concern of scams in the community.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This means that more Singaporeans have fallen victim to various scams last year.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Breaking down the statistics on the top contact methods which scammers employees shows that messaging and social media platforms form the two largest group of contact methods favoured by scammers.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We know that our Home Team is making it a key priority and working hard to combat scams and cybercrime.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This House has also passed various legislation to provide the Home Team with the necessary powers to address this issue.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: On the other hand, however, as responsible corporate entities, we do not hear much of the efforts of the messaging and social platforms in utilising the information they have in the operations to support the fight against scams.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As such media platforms, leverage on their membership and user numbers to monetise revenue, it is only right for them to put, in a commensurate amount of effort in also protecting the interests of their members and users.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: One of the reasons why scammers are successful is because law enforcement is also left chasing the tails of scammers.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I say these because the scammers are adept and extremely quick in changing tactics or deploying a different method as soon as they realise that law enforcement or the public have caught on to their ruse.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There are also certain scam tactics that seemed to remain evergreen such as job scams, fake friend call scams or phishing scams.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Yet even within these so-called established categories of scams, scammers evolve their own methodology very often.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Apart from law enforcement working harder, smarter and quicker with various stakeholders to catch perpetrators of scams or break up scams syndicates, I think their public education also plays an important role in preventing scams.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Perhaps the most straightforward way to prevent scams is for an informed citizenry not to fall victim to scams.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I invite the Minister to update us on how the Ministry can better inform and educate the public on the evolving tactics of these scammers.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: My Clementi resident got scammed, life savings gone.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: She faces bankruptcy and if so, she will lose her job.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Someone in Singapore allowed their bank account to be used as a runner's bank account to take my resident's money, send it overseas beyond retrieval.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: How many money mules or scam runners actually get caught?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The runners have done their calculations and many are not deterred.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Last year, scam cases went up 10% year on year, but can MHA's Anti-Scam hotline and the Anti-Scam Command, can they hire 10% more officers every year indefinitely?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: A very serious problem calls for very serious measures.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Let us look at how the government has handled unlicensed moneylending.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The Moneylenders Act states that if someone's bank account is used to facilitate unlicensed moneylending, they are deemed to have assisted the illegal business.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Offenders can face jail, fine or even caning.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Today, if a loan shark runner handles $10,000 of cash, taken from a victim, they can be caned.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But a scammer or scam runner, if they make off with $100,000 of someone's life savings, from a scam victim, they cannot be caned.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have Clementi residents wondering, is Singapore too soft on scammers?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Let us say the runner knew it was organised crime, knew the bank account would be used to take people's money for scams and send it overseas.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For intermediate cases, discretionary caning, depending on the facts of the case.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In short, Mr Chairman, we must send a clear message to scammers, the syndicates and those who abet them, if you mess with our people, make off with the life savings of Singaporeans, scams Singaporeans, we must do everything in our power to teach the scammers a lesson they would not forget.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Will the Minister send that message to the scammers and those who assist them in taking our residents' life savings?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Derrick Goh, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: But as our society becomes increasingly digital, the challenge of scams grows ever more complex.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In 2024, we have made considerable progress against this stress.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This underscores the adaptive nature of scammers, who not only exploit human vulnerabilities, such as desperation during job hunts or emotional appeals in fraudulent investments, but are also leveraging technologies like AI and deepfakes to further their illicit activities.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As scammers evolve, so too must our strategies.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: First, while significant measures have been implemented, including restricting movement of potential victims' monies with the recently passed Protection from Scams Bill, what additional proactive steps can be taken to stem the scourge of scams?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Are there plans to strengthen interagency and inter-sector collaborations to pre-empt emerging scam tactics?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Considering the substantial financial losses incurred, what is MHA's assessment of our effectiveness in recovering scam proceeds and how can efforts be further improved?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Third, as scammers exploit advanced technologies such as AI to deploy more convincing fraudulent schemes, what new approaches or legislative frameworks will be introduced to counter these developments?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: How can our existing technological tools, like the Scam Analytics and Tactical Intervention System, be improved to disrupt emerging scam enablers, including fraudulent mobile numbers and payment channels?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, how may public education efforts be more targeted to focus on high-loss scam types?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Chairman, fire safety is critical to safeguarding lives and property.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: These statistics highlight the growing risks associated with AMDs, particularly as they become more prevalent in our daily lives.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Over the course of 2024, I assisted several of my residents in Nee Soon Link who suffered injuries and whose flat suffered damages due to fires.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I commend the efforts of the Singapore Civil Defence Force and the Land Transport Authority in assisting these areas.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The refreshed campaign underscores the importance of raising awareness about safe charging practices and the proper use of batteries.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: However, given the rising number of AMD fires, I feel more can be done to mitigate these risks.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, my questions are: how can MHA further enhance public education efforts to ensure these safety messages reach more users effectively?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Are there plans to tighten regulations on the sale and use of non-compliant or non-original AMD batteries, which are key contributors to the risk?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: How can enforcement and inspection measures at retail points and online marketplaces be strengthened to deter the sale of unsafe devices and components?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: We must continue to educate and regulate effectively to keep our homes and communities safe.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I am speaking up on behalf of all healthcare workers, whether nursing or non-nursing, who are having to care for and handle patients with mental health conditions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I am aware that the Ministry of Health has worked out a tripartite advisory on harassment of healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: However, this feedback is gathered in my engagements with healthcare workers and management at the Institute of Mental Health (IMH) as they have daily face-to-face time with both physical and non-physical contact with patients with behavioural issues.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: There have been numerous cases where nurses, staff and even fellow patients had been injured due to sudden and sporadic display of violent and disorderly behaviour of a small proportion of patients.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: These are clearly recorded cases and sometimes, unarmed private security or even the auxiliary police officers themselves could not act on them and have to call in the police.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I therefore ask for MHA to review the existing legislation, both the main statues and subsidiary legislation such as the Penal Code, Prevention of Harassment Act as well as the Destitute Persons Act, and explore working with IMH to eradicate or if not, minimise the occurrence of such incidents, which affects workplace health and safety of patients, healthcare staff and outsourced workers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Members for their support of the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA).

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: My colleagues and I will address the points that they raised.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Minister of State Sun Xueling will speak about our multi-pronged approach to tackle scams.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Minister of State Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim will touch on our rehabilitative initiatives, including for drug abusers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I will provide an update on the Ministry's transformation for a future-oriented and trusted Home Team.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Over the years, the Home Team has embarked on numerous transformation initiatives.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum asked about our progress.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Risk assessments can now be conducted ahead of the passengers' arrival, enabling ICA to better identify travellers with possible security or immigration risks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the same time, with passport-less clearance at Changi Airport, the traveller experience has improved significantly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The traveller just has to face the screen, without needing to also scan the passport.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: NCC has also transformed the job of the ICA officer.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They no longer spend most of their time opening, checking and stamping passports.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With reskilling, they now perform higher value-added work to safeguard Singapore's borders, such as profiling travellers as they go through the automated lanes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the past, each manual counter needed to be manned by an individual officer.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Criminals are exploiting technology, in particular, artificial intelligence (AI), to carry out more sophisticated crimes and to hit more victims.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Birth rates are declining and the competition for talent very tough.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Home Team departments have been reviewing and reprioritising operations, policies and other work.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Despite these efforts, the pressures on the Home Team remains intense.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain asked about the measures to deal with technology-enabled crime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To stay ahead, the Home Team has been taking bold steps to leverage technology in our mission, in particular, using AI against AI-enabled crime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Last year, the Home Team Science and Technology Agency (HTX) launched the Home Team AI Movement to accelerate the development and delivery of AI capabilities across the Home Team.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have started to use some of these AI solutions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: One example is the Singapore Civil Defence Force's (SCDF's) Targeted On-site Inspection Tool, which is an AI model to assess the likelihood of fire safety violations in commercial and industrial premises, using data from various sources, including past inspection reports.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The tool will be progressively rolled out to frontline units for field testing in the coming months.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It will allow SCDF to optimise its resources, by carrying out inspections on a more targeted basis.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Other than AI, the Home Team is also leveraging smart and autonomous solutions to detect threats earlier and respond faster.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, Singapore Prisons is trialling the use of smart sensors in its medical wards and cells to monitor inmates' vital signs remotely.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The system will enable Prison officers to respond more quickly to incidents, such as falls and abnormal heart rates, among the inmates.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is especially important with a growing pool of older inmates.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As criminals adopt more advanced modus operandi, our criminal justice procedures and processes must also be more nimble and effective to deal with new types of cybercrime, as well as the increased speed and scale at which cybercrimes are being committed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will continue to: review our laws, to ensure their ability to deal with traditional crimes committed in cyberspace; and strengthen our regulatory frameworks, to better leverage technology to combat cybercrimes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, with the rapid proliferation of websites that facilitate scams and other malicious cyber activities, the Government is considering how to use technology to autonomously disrupt such websites more rapidly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Gen AI has the potential to improve operational effectiveness and efficiency, for us to better serve Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But as with many other technologies, it comes with risks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Just as the Home Team seeks to use Gen AI to improve our work, criminals are also abusing the same technology to prey on innocent victims.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, scammers are exploiting Gen AI to produce fake content at speed and scale, and to target victims.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They can also use it to manufacture evidence to mislead or frustrate investigators.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are therefore developing capabilities, to detect and identify AI-generated scams and falsified content.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, AlchemiX, a Gen AI-powered algorithm, has been developed to identify whether audio or video recordings are genuine.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our capabilities must be backed by strong legislative frameworks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Designated online service providers are already required to implement measures to proactively disrupt online scams, including those facilitated by AI.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will continually assess if they need to do more.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A second risk is when we use Gen AI to support decision-making.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: What if the model was trained using data that was illegally obtained?

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: What if the model produces outputs that are biased against certain groups?

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We take them seriously and have put in place an AI Governance Framework to guide the implementation of AI projects and ensure compliance with our laws, such as ensuring fair, representative and responsible use of data.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will also put in place safeguards, including to ensure that there is an appropriate level of human intervention to act as a layer of checks and ensure accountability.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In addition to these risks, Ms He Ting Ru highlighted AI-generated crime that are violent in nature.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I agree with her that the risks to children and women are particularly concerning.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are thus moving quickly to deal with these risks robustly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: More details will be announced in due course.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As for the new legislation and agency to tackle online harms, I will be providing more information during the Ministry of Digital Development and Innovation's (MDDI's) Committee of Supply (COS) debate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: While technological capabilities are important, they are not enough.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We also need to ensure that Home Team officers are well-trained to use the technologies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As part of the Home Team AI Movement, HTX is developing an AI training roadmap to empower officers across all our agencies to use AI tools effectively.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Singapore Police Force (SPF) has also implemented a cybercrime competency framework to provide its officers with the skillsets to tackle rapidly-evolving cybercrimes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To Ms He's suggestion, I am pleased to share that training programmes have been provided to better support our Police officers in dealing with sexual crime cases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A training roadmap has also been implemented for officers managing sexual crime and family violence cases, to equip them with the necessary skills to handle these sensitive cases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: One key area that has been significantly impacted is SCDF's Emergency Medical Services (EMS).

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar asked how we are coping.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We expect it to spike further as our population ages.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: SCDF has therefore expanded its recruitment pathways for EMS officers, including through the SCDF-Institute of Technical Education (ITE) Work-Study Diploma.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is in Paramedicine and it offers applicants an opportunity to begin a career with SCDF while pursuing a diploma.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To recognise, develop and retain deep expertise in the EMS domain, SCDF also introduced the Paramedicine Expert Track.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They will enable SCDF to build domain knowledge in the EMS field, mentor junior paramedics and improve EMS protocols.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In recognition of their expertise and additional contributions to SCDF, the senior specialists will receive an additional allowance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Despite these efforts and more competitive salaries, local recruitment is insufficient to meet all our needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is because EMS roles require advanced medical skills that are in short supply locally.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Also, EMS work, although very fulfilling, is very challenging and may not appeal to all.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: All new recruits, regardless of nationality, will undergo rigorous training and accreditation, including to obtain the necessary professional qualifications, in accordance with SCDF's standards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is to ensure that SCDF continues to deliver the highest standards of emergency medical services to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the same time, SCDF will continue to focus on recruiting Singaporeans, to maintain a strong local core.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Last January, we also shared in Parliament that MHA may allow our Auxiliary Police Forces (APFs) to recruit foreign Auxiliary Police Officers (APOs) from more sources.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Singaporeans make up the majority of APOs and will remain so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To ensure that safety and security standards are not compromised, all APOs, regardless of nationality, must meet the physical, educational and probity requirements set by the Singapore Police Force.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This includes passing security screening and the APO basic course.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The APFs also ensure that the new APOs become familiar with Singapore's local context, cultural nuances and operating environment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain asked how we are updating our efforts to harness the support of the community in keeping Singapore safe and secure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In May last year, SPF launched the Cyber Guardians on Watch initiative, to enlist the help of the public to tackle cybercrimes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Cyber Guardians receive advisories from the Police, for dissemination to their own networks and communities, to raise awareness of online scams and other cybercrimes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They also act as the Police's eyes and ears in the cyberspace and will alert the Police to any suspicious activity online.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Since 1 January this year, more than 32,000 members have been helping to make cyberspace safer for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Overall, the Home Team has achieved good outcomes for our people.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These are reflected in how Singaporeans view the Home Team positively and hold our officers in high regard.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many have also stepped forward to volunteer and assist in our crime prevention efforts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These attitudes are indicative of a high level of trust between the public and the Home Team, which as Mr Zhulkarnain mentioned, is lacking in many other jurisdictions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will continue our efforts to build understanding and trust with the public.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, with your permission, I would like to conclude my remarks in Mandarin.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Minister of State Assoc Prof Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Chairman, I will now speak on the drug situation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This amount is almost 8,000 times the amount seized in Singapore that year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Drug abuse threatens public safety and impacts innocent victims, as those under the influence of drugs may resort to crime to feed their habit, or commit violence against others.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Even though Singapore's drug situation is under control, we still have drug-related crimes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We are an attractive market for drug traffickers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Our purchasing power means that the street price of drugs in Singapore can be many times higher than in other countries, allowing traffickers to reap massive profits.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Singapore has in place tough laws and effective enforcement to curb drug supply.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: More importantly, we also focus on reducing demand through, firstly, creating strong public awareness of the harms of drugs through preventive drug education (PDE); and secondly, helping drug abusers turn over a new leaf through evidence-based rehabilitation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Vikram Nair pointed out that the number of young drug abusers is on the rise.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This is an area of concern for us.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Nair and Ms Mariam Jaafar ask how we can inoculate youths against the harms of drugs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will continue to expand our PDE efforts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The Inter-Ministry Committee on Drug Prevention for Youth will focus on the following areas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: First, strengthening our network of over 1000 DrugFreeSG champions, comprising of educators, counsellors, youths and healthcare workers who help disseminate drug-free messages in the community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will enhance their skills and knowledge with training.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In March 2025, we will organise a DrugFreeSG Champions Conference to equip the DrugFreeSG Champions with insights on drug matters.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Second, continuing to promote anti-drug awareness through the Drug Victims' Remembrance Day.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The inaugural Remembrance Day held last year had a very good turnout and over 100,000 pledges to be drug-free were logged.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will also continue collaborating with schools and parents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: All schools will continue to conduct at least one PDE programme annually.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The Ministry of Education (MOE) will work with the Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB) to invite Parent Support Group leaders to participate in capability building sessions on drug-related topics and will continue making PDE resources available for all parents on the Parents Gateway Portal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Besides preventing drug abuse among the young, it is also important to rehabilitate drug abusers to wean off their drug addiction.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: To this end, CNB piloted the "Supervision 2.0" regime in January 2024 for ex-drug abusers who are placed under supervision upon release from Drug Rehabilitation Centres.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Under this pilot, hair analysis tests are used as the default monitoring mechanism for CNB's supervisors, as it can detect drug abuse over a longer period compared to urine tests.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Supervisees can then report to the reporting centre less frequently, reducing disruption to their daily lives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum also asked how we can prepare ex-drug abusers for successful re-integration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Under Supervision 2.0, supervisees will undergo Community Supervision Sessions where the CNB supervision officer will check in on the supervisee's well-being, the progress of interventions and assess the supervisee's residual re-integration needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: CNB can then refer the supervisees to the appropriate agencies for support, such as for assistance with housing or employment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The preliminary findings from the pilot are positive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: CNB was able to swiftly detect more supervisees who had relapsed via hair tests as compared to under the urine supervision regime, due to the longer detection windows for hair tests.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: About two-thirds of the supervisees rated the scheme as "very helpful" in their re-integration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I will now move on to other rehabilitation and re-integration efforts for inmates and ex-offenders, which Mr Patrick Tay, Assoc Prof Razwana and Ms Jean See have filed cuts on.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Assoc Prof Razwana asked how these efforts account for the specific needs of female drug abusers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Prisons incorporates trauma-informed practises in their psychology-based correctional programmes for all women inmates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: These programmes teach inmates to replace unhealthy ways of coping with past trauma, like drug abuse, with techniques to regulate their emotions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Prisons currently works with 20 family-focused partners to deliver structured family programmes, benefiting more than 3,000 inmates and families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Prisons is conducting a trial of the Family Engagement model, which aims to strengthen the ability of inmates and their family in building and maintaining relationships through family re-integration programmes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Inmates will also attend support group sessions led by community partners and peer supporters who had completed the programme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This allows inmates to shift their identity away from being offenders to being role models.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Since 2022, Prisons has collaborated with schools to pilot Project Hope, in which video visits are conducted between incarcerated parents and school-going children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This initiative allows inmates to stay involved in their children's lives and understand their progress in school.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The pilot participants have experienced improvements in their relationships and the schools have also observed positive changes in the students' behaviour and emotional well-being.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Prisons is working with MOE to expand Project Hope to more schools.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The centralised facility allows Prisons to better implement targeted re-integration-centric programmes. for suitable inmates, such as those emplaced on community-based programmes prior to release.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The Re-integration Hub provides easier physical access for community partners and volunteers to support the inmates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: They need not travel to separate prison institutions on separate occasions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The Hub has also implemented pre-emplacement programmes, which include sharing sessions with desistors, to provide motivation and encouragement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will also equip inmates with relevant skills to navigate an increasingly digitalised world, which can impede re-integration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The Access for Inmate Digital Experience (AIDE) is a new initiative to allow inmates to familiarise themselves with, and independently access citizenry e-services, such as those provided by the Central Provident Fund (CPF) Board, and the Housing and Development Board (HDB), during incarceration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Another pillar of our re-integration strategy is to equip ex-offenders with market-relevant work skills.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Ms See asked what more we can do in this regard.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Yellow Ribbon Singapore (YRSG) will be enhancing its career facilitation efforts, in particular to assist ex-offenders attain their career goals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This includes refining "Career Circles", which was piloted in 2023.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The "Career Circles" programme comprises facilitated sessions on various career-related topics, such as career planning and addressing common workplace challenges.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Inmates are equipped with the skills to set career goals and prepare for job searches.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The enhanced version of "Career Circles" with a revised curriculum and frequency was implemented from February 2025.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Tay asked if the spent regime for criminal records could be reviewed to further support ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: MHA periodically reviews the spend regime for criminal records.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: An ex-offender could have his offence spent as early as five years, if he or she stays crime-free during this period and fulfils the criteria set out in the Registration of Criminals Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Our current assessment is that the criteria and regime remain appropriate in striking the balance between the interest of the ex-offenders, employers and society at large.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Assoc Prof Razwana asked how partnerships with social services and the broader community can complement MHA's rehabilitation and re-integration efforts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The Community Action for Rehabilitation of Ex-offenders Network (CARE Network) was formed in May 2000 by an alliance of 10 core members, comprising Government organisations and social service agencies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: It has since expanded to coordinate the efforts of over a hundred community partners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In 2023, more than 16,000 beneficiaries benefited from the services provided by CARE Network agencies, such as financial assistance and skills training.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I offer my congratulations to the CARE Network, which will be celebrating its 25th anniversary this year and will be unveiling its work plan for the next five years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The network has provided an invaluable service to society in assisting and transforming the lives of ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Prisons and YRSG also work with more than 4,200 volunteers to address the rehabilitation and re-integration needs of both inmates and ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Over 6,700 employers have also partnered with YRSG to hire ex-offenders, which is an almost 20% increase from 2021 to 2024.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Prisons has enhanced its volunteer training framework, called "Igniting and Maximising Partners' Agility for Correctional Transformation" (IMPACT).

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: IMPACT aims to develop the competencies of volunteers and community partners, by introducing structured and tiered training pathways.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In 2024, more than 1,800 volunteers were trained under IMPACT.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Assoc Prof Razwana asked how we can increase support for the halfway house regime.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In 2024, our halfway house partners provided step-down support for more than 1,200 offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Under HSM+, supervisees will undergo a longer duration of aftercare support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Halfway house staff will be equipped with skills to work effectively with different profiles of supervisees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Infrastructural works will also be carried out to improve accessibility for those with mobility issues.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I will now speak in Malay on the role of Malay/Muslim Organisations (MMOs) in our rehabilitation efforts. :   Sir, MHA collaborates with various Malay/Muslim Organisations (MMO) to provide relevant support to our Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In 2024, CNB launched a new grant in collaboration with MUIS.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This grant will provide a source of funding for mosques to organise programmes that support prevention of drugs efforts (PDE) under the DrugFreeSG and “Dadah Itu Haram” campaigns.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Ten such events have been organised, including the Anti-Drug Forum run by the Hasanah Mosque for parents and youths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Our MMO partners also continue to actively strengthen their relationship with one another, in order to build a strong network to support offenders and ex-inmates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will also work with community partners to streamline training for new volunteers involved in providing faith-based counselling.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This will facilitate inter-agency coordination to enable agencies to better meet the beneficiaries' needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I will move on to address Members' cuts on road safety.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked how we can improve public participation in our road safety efforts, such as encouraging the reporting of dangerous driving practices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We urge the public to report traffic violations via our e-Feedback on Road User portal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We have observed a consistent upward trend of such reports since the portal's introduction.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Singh suggested re-introducing speed warning lights on the top of commercial vehicles.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Those lights were mandated of light goods vehicles in the early 1980s.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Since April 2001, such lights were no longer required by the Land Transport Authority (LTA) due to feedback that they increased the overall height of the vehicle, causing accessibility issues into carparks, which was both an inconvenience and safety hazard.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: On balance, we do not think we should re-introduce such lights.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will instead rely on other means of detecting speeding vehicles, such as more speed cameras.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked if the licence renewal process for seniors could be improved.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Currently, two letters are sent – 10 weeks and four weeks before the driver's 65th birthday, to remind them to complete the necessary procedures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: If they have not done so by their 65th birthday, their licence ceases to be valid, and the Traffic Police sends them a third letter.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The third letter will inform the drivers to submit their medical report within three years to reinstate the licence, failing which, they would have to apply anew for a licence, including going through the various tests.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We believe the current process provides sufficient notice and time to the driver to comply with the requirement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In 2024, the Traffic Police redesigned the notification letters to use visual aids, making it easier for seniors to understand what they need to do.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim also asked if the medical examination requirement for seniors to renew their licence can be deferred to a later age.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Any increase in the age at which a medical examination is required would need to take into consideration the possible adverse impact on the safety of other road users.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We do not plan to do so at this time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Before I end, let me also address Mr Derrick Goh's cut on mitigating the fire risks posed by Active Mobility Devices, or AMDs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The Active Mobility Fire Safety Taskforce, co-chaired by LTA and SCDF, launched the "Be Device-Safe" programme in 2023.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The programme educates users of motorised AMDs the risk of AMD-related fires and how to safely procure, use, maintain and dispose of such devices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In September 2024, we unveiled a refreshed campaign with new visuals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: SCDF will also continue to disseminate advisories on AMD fires via social media and mainstream media.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The Ministry of Transport's (MOT's) COS debate will further address enforcement measures against AMDs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Last year, we encouraged Members of this House to show your support by wearing the green-and-white ribbon for a drug-free Singapore and the yellow ribbon for giving second chances to ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This year, we seek your continued support by wearing the ribbons again, which can be collected at the Parliament Library.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Mr Chairman, scams are a huge concern globally, as they are in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We have been fighting the scourge of scams for several years now.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We have progressively strengthened our defences, from enhancing banking apps to be malware-resistant, to blocking calls from known scam numbers and labelling SMSes that are likely to be scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In 2024 alone, SPF disrupted more than 150,000 scam-related mobile and WhatsApp lines, websites and online accounts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Many people are rightly very concerned about this and so is the Government.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We must and we will redouble our efforts in this fight against scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We are up against highly organised and sophisticated criminal networks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: They are well-resourced, adept at using technology and constantly evolve their tactics to evade our defences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Government will continue to respond aggressively to this challenge.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This accounts for more than 80% of scam losses last year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In many cases, victims thought they were transferring money to friends, Government officials, e-commerce sellers or for legitimate investment opportunities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Gone are the days when we could easily spot a scam call or email, through heavy foreign accents or bad English.
